narrative:
The model predicted a 57% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically denied your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. This consistent low academic standing in law school was the main reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.70 also worked against you, though with less force. Both fell noticeably below the averages of accepted students (37.2 on the LSAT and 3.23 GPA), nudging the prediction further toward failure. Your middle family income, full-time study plan, gender, and Hispanic background played no role in the outcome; the system did not consider them.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank through targeted study support or tutoring, and consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction. Many students successfully reapply after strengthening exactly these areas.
